content: For instance, participant ages can be grouped into ranges of 5–10 years. Survey protocols should specify whether the collected data will be shared with other researchers. Regulations governing human subjects may require similar details to be included in the consent forms. Investigators must determine whether institutional regulations, funder policies, or national guidelines recommend or discourage data sharing. This chapter discusses the rationale and methods for providing third-party researchers with access to individual-level data from biobehavioral surveys (BBS). Since most BBS are publicly funded and collect data from public subpopulations, the public has a right to be informed of the survey findings and, with appropriate safeguards, to access and use the data. Sharing anonymized individual-level survey data free of charge is considered good public health practice, as it maximizes the utility of the survey. Data sharing allows other researchers to explore questions or analyses that the original investigators may not have considered. Decisions about data accessibility should be guided by national data confidentiality regulations and standards. Data-use agreements should outline the requirements for accessing and using the data. Alternatively, they can provide the raw data along with cleaning codes and the resulting clean data files to enhance transparency in data management. Secondary variables may be added to facilitate analysis. Reference documents should accompany the shared data to provide context, including a data dictionary, survey instruments, survey protocol, guidance for proper attribution, and investigator contact information. The data dictionary should explain response values and variable labels, while the survey instruments should include the full phrasing of questions and responses, as well as skip patterns. The survey protocol should detail the sampling design, eligibility criteria, and other critical design elements. Public-use datasets must be stripped of personally identifiable information, such as dates of birth (day and month), photographic images, email addresses, phone numbers, street addresses, and social security or other identification numbers. Geographic information, such as place of residence, should either be grouped into larger areas or removed entirely. Reporting standards should be established to guide third-party researchers in protecting participant identities, such as avoiding the presentation of data for cells with fewer than five participants. Survey data should be made available as soon as possible after collection. Some agencies may have policies requiring data release within a specific timeframe following survey completion. Websites dedicated to hosting and sharing research and survey data enable third-party researchers to access these datasets. These websites typically provide information about policies for accessing and using the data, including the required format and accompanying metadata. Researchers can access the data by adhering to the website’s rules and regulations. In most cases, users must sign a data-use agreement to gain access, although for some datasets, downloading the data implies consent to the agreement. For an example of a data-use agreement, refer to Appendix I-37. References: 1. Bernstein AB, Sweeney MH. Public health surveillance data: legal, policy, ethical, regulatory, and practical issues. MMWR Surveill Summ. 2012;61:30–34.
